title: Rocks and Fossils
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Earth and space
summary: Learn to identify igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks from their features, and how fossils form in sedimentary rock — with diagrams, worked examples and a Checkpoint-style quiz.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Know that rocks can be sorted into three types — igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic — and describe the features that help you identify each type (6ESp.01).
Describe how fossils can form in sedimentary rocks (6ESp.02).
Skills from Thinking and Working Scientifically used on this page: using a key to identify rocks, testing rocks (hardness, water absorption), and recording results in a table.

blocks.text: 1. What is a rock?

A **rock** is a natural solid made of **minerals**. If you look at a rock with a hand lens you will see that it is made either of **crystals** that fit tightly together, or of **grains** (small pieces) that are stuck together. How the crystals or grains look tells you how the rock was made — and that is how scientists sort rocks into three groups.

rows: Melted rock (magma or lava) cools and becomes solid
'Ignis' means fire — it was once melted by great heat
Layers of sediment are buried, pressed and cemented together
'Sediment' — bits that settle at the bottom of water
An existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting

blocks.text: 2. Igneous rocks

Deep underground the rock is so hot that some of it melts. This melted rock is called **magma**. When magma reaches the surface (for example from a volcano) it is called **lava**. When magma or lava cools down it **solidifies** (becomes solid) and forms **igneous rock**.

items: **Interlocking crystals** — the crystals grow into each other as the liquid cools, so there are no gaps between them.
Crystals point in **random directions** — they are **not** in layers or bands.
Usually **hard** and **not porous** (water does not soak in), because there are no gaps between the crystals.
**No fossils** — anything living would have been destroyed by the great heat of the melted rock.

**Crystal size tells you the cooling speed:** magma that cools **slowly** deep underground has time to grow **large crystals** (granite); lava that cools **quickly** on the surface forms **small crystals** (basalt). Lava that cools extremely quickly may form glass with no crystals at all (obsidian).

rows: Large crystals you can see easily (often pink, white and black); very hard
Dark grey or black; crystals too small to see without a lens
Black and shiny like glass; no crystals
Quickly, from frothy lava full of gas
Full of holes from gas bubbles; so light it can float

blocks.title: Egypt connection
blocks.text: The ancient Egyptians cut **granite** at **Aswan** for obelisks and statues because it is so hard and lasts for thousands of years. Granite is an igneous rock — look closely at an Aswan statue and you can see its large interlocking crystals.

blocks.alt: Close-up of pink, white and dark crystals in Aswan granite
blocks.caption: Pink granite from Aswan close up: large pink, white and dark crystals fit tightly together in random directions — the sign of an igneous rock that cooled slowly.
blocks.credit: Photo: Glenn Ashton / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.text: 3. Sedimentary rocks

Rivers carry small pieces of rock, sand, mud and shells into lakes and seas. These pieces, called **sediment**, settle at the bottom in flat **layers**. Over thousands and millions of years new layers bury the older ones. The weight of the layers on top **presses** (compacts) the lower layers, squeezes out the water, and natural minerals **cement** the grains together. The sediment slowly becomes **sedimentary rock**.

items: Made of **grains**, often rounded (they were rubbed smooth while being carried by water or wind).
Found in **layers** (strata).
May contain **fossils**.
Often **porous** — there are tiny gaps between the grains, so the rock soaks up water.
Often **soft or crumbly** — grains can be rubbed off with a finger or scratched with a nail.

rows: Gritty feel; grains you can see; porous
Mostly shells and skeletons of sea creatures
Often contains fossils; fizzes with acid such as vinegar
Tiny shells of microscopic sea creatures
White, soft, leaves a mark on your fingers
Very fine grains; shale splits into thin layers

blocks.title: Egypt connection
blocks.text: Most of the blocks of the **Pyramids of Giza** are **limestone**, a sedimentary rock. If you look closely, you can see thousands of small round fossils called **nummulites** — the shells of tiny sea creatures. This tells us that the Giza area was once under the sea.

blocks.alt: A coin-shaped nummulite fossil split open to show its coiled chambers
blocks.caption: A nummulite fossil split open to show the coiled chambers of its shell; fossils like this can be seen in many of the limestone blocks of the Giza pyramids.

blocks.text: 4. Metamorphic rocks

When a rock is buried very deep, or is close to hot magma, it is heated and squeezed. The rock does **not melt**, but its minerals change and grow into new crystals. The new rock is a **metamorphic rock**. Any type of rock — igneous, sedimentary or even another metamorphic rock — can be changed in this way.

items: Made of **crystals**, often lined up in **bands, stripes or thin sheets** because the rock was squeezed in one direction.
Usually **very hard** and **not porous**.
**Fossils are usually destroyed** (squashed and changed) by the heat and pressure.
Remember: **heat and pressure, but NOT melting**. If the rock melts, it becomes magma, and the rock that forms later is igneous.

rows: Sparkly, sugary-looking crystals; can be white or coloured; no fossils
Dark grey; splits into thin flat sheets (used for roof tiles)
Very hard; sand grains have joined into crystals
Clear light and dark bands of crystals

blocks.alt: A piece of gneiss with wavy light and dark stripes
blocks.caption: Gneiss, a metamorphic rock: heat and pressure lined its crystals up into light and dark bands.
blocks.credit: Photo: Siim / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.text: 5. Identifying a rock: use a key

In Checkpoint you may be given a key or asked to use the features of a rock to name its type. Look first for **layers, grains and fossils** (sedimentary). If there are crystals, check whether they are **lined up in bands** (metamorphic) or **random and interlocking** (igneous).

blocks.text: Scientists also use simple **tests**:

rows: Use a hand lens to look at the grains or crystals
Rounded grains → sedimentary; random interlocking crystals → igneous; crystals in bands → metamorphic
Try to scratch the rock with a fingernail, then an iron nail
Soft rocks that scratch easily are often sedimentary (e.g. chalk); igneous and metamorphic rocks are usually hard
Drop water on the rock, or weigh the rock dry and again after soaking it
If the water soaks in (or the mass increases), the rock is porous — usually sedimentary
Rub the rock with a finger or another rock

blocks.title: Safety
items: Wear eye protection when scratching or breaking rocks — small chips can fly off.
Wash your hands after handling rocks and do not taste them.

blocks.text: 6. Fossils
A **fossil** is the remains or trace of a plant or animal that lived a very long time ago (usually millions of years), preserved in rock. Fossils can be:

items: **body fossils** — the hard parts of a living thing, such as bones, teeth, shells or wood, that have been turned into rock;
**trace fossils** — signs that a living thing was there, such as footprints, burrows or droppings;
**moulds and casts** — a shell dissolves and leaves a hole the same shape (a mould); if minerals later fill the hole, they make a rock copy of the shell (a cast).

blocks.caption: The four main stages of fossil formation (simple drawing, not to scale).

items: A plant or animal **dies** and falls to the bottom of a sea, lake or river.
The **soft parts rot** away or are eaten. The **hard parts** (bones, teeth, shells) are left.
The remains are **quickly buried** by sediment such as mud or sand. This protects them from animals, from rotting and from being broken by moving water.
More and more layers of sediment build up on top. Their **weight presses** the lower layers and they slowly turn into **sedimentary rock**.
Water containing **dissolved minerals** seeps through the rock. The minerals slowly **replace** the bone or shell, making a rock copy — a fossil. (Or the shell dissolves and leaves a mould.)
Millions of years later, movements of the Earth **lift** the rock up and **erosion** (wind, rain, rivers) wears away the rock above, so the fossil is exposed at the surface where people can find it.

blocks.text: Why are fossils found in sedimentary rocks?

rows: Sediment settles gently and buries remains without destroying them
It forms from melted rock — the great heat destroys any remains
High heat and pressure squash and change the remains

blocks.text: Fossils are **rare**. Most living things are eaten or rot away before they can be buried, and animals with no hard parts (such as worms or jellyfish) hardly ever leave fossils.
What fossils tell us

items: **What lived long ago** — including living things that are now extinct, such as dinosaurs and ammonites.

**What the place was like** — sea shells in desert rock show that the area was once under the sea. At **Wadi El-Hitan** (the Valley of the Whales) in Fayoum, Egypt, there are skeletons of ancient whales, around 40 million years old, in what is now desert.

**Which rocks are older** — sediment is laid down one layer on top of another, so in undisturbed rock the **lowest layers are the oldest** and fossils in them lived earlier than fossils in the layers above.

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية بالعربي
items: الصخر الناري (igneous): بيتكوّن لما الصهارة أو الحمم تبرد وتتجمد — بلورات متداخلة، مافيهوش طبقات ولا حفريات.
الصخر الرسوبي (sedimentary): رواسب بتترسب في طبقات وتتضغط وتلتصق — حبيبات وطبقات وممكن فيه حفريات.
الصخر المتحول (metamorphic): صخر اتغير بالحرارة والضغط من غير ما يدوب — بلورات في خطوط أو أشرطة.
الحفريات بتتكوّن في الصخور الرسوبية بس تقريبًا، لأن الحرارة في الصخر الناري والمتحول بتدمرها.

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Three rock samples are described below. Name the type of rock for each one. [3 marks]

rows: Hard; large crystals of different colours that fit tightly together in random directions
Layers of rounded sand grains; soaks up water; a shell is visible
Very hard; crystals lined up in dark and light stripes

items: X has random **interlocking crystals** and no layers → **igneous** (1 mark).
Y has **layers**, **rounded grains**, is **porous** and has a **fossil** → **sedimentary** (1 mark).
Z has crystals in **bands** → **metamorphic** (1 mark).

blocks.text: Common mistake: calling Z igneous because it has crystals. Ask yourself: are the crystals **random** (igneous) or **lined up** (metamorphic)?
**Worked example 2** — Granite and basalt are both igneous rocks. Granite has large crystals and basalt has small crystals. Explain this difference. [2 marks]

items: Granite formed from magma that cooled **slowly** deep underground, so the crystals had time to grow large (1 mark).
Basalt formed from lava that cooled **quickly** on the surface, so the crystals did not have time to grow (1 mark).

blocks.text: Common mistake: writing 'granite is bigger'. The marks are for linking **cooling speed** to **crystal size**.
**Worked example 3** — Describe how the skeleton of a fish could become a fossil. [3 marks]

items: The fish dies, sinks to the sea bed and the soft parts rot away (1 mark).
The bones are quickly buried by layers of sediment, which are pressed together into sedimentary rock (1 mark).
Minerals slowly replace the bones, making a rock copy of the skeleton (1 mark).

blocks.text: Exam tip: use the key words **buried**, **sediment**, **layers**, **minerals replace**. Three marks means three separate points.
**Worked example 4** — Omar wants to find out which rock is the most porous. He weighs each rock dry, soaks it in water for one hour, then weighs it again.

(a) Work out the mass of water soaked up by the sandstone. [1 mark] (b) Which rock is the most porous? Explain your answer. [1 mark] (c) Give one thing Omar kept the same to make this a fair test. [1 mark]

items: (b) **Chalk** — it soaked up the most water (58 − 50 = 8 g).
(c) Any one: the same starting mass of rock (50 g) / the same soaking time (one hour) / the same water.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — A fossil shark tooth is found in a rock. (a) What type of rock is it most likely to be? (b) Give a reason. [2 marks]

items: (a) **Sedimentary** (1 mark).
(b) Fossils form when remains are buried in sediment; the heat in igneous and metamorphic rocks would destroy them (1 mark).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying metamorphic rocks form by **melting**. They form by **heat and pressure without melting**. Melting leads to magma and then igneous rock.
Saying igneous rocks have **layers**. Layers are a feature of sedimentary rock (bands of crystals = metamorphic).
Mixing up **grains** (pieces stuck together — sedimentary) and **crystals** (grown together — igneous and metamorphic).
Writing that a fossil is 'a dead animal'. A fossil is the remains or trace **preserved in rock**, usually millions of years old.
Forgetting that the remains must be **buried quickly** — otherwise they rot or are eaten.
Thinking the top layer of rock is the oldest. In undisturbed layers the **bottom** layer is the oldest.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Name the rock type** from a description, a picture or a table of features — look for the key words: crystals, interlocking, layers, grains, fossils, bands.
**Use or complete a key** — follow each question in order; do not jump to the end.
**Explain** a feature: always link the feature to how the rock formed (e.g. small crystals → cooled quickly).
**Put the stages of fossil formation in order**, or describe them — buried → layers → rock → minerals replace → uplift and erosion.
**Investigation questions:** variables in a porosity or scratch test, reading a results table, working out a change in mass (after − before).
One mark usually needs one clear idea. For 'explain' questions give the idea **and** the reason.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Rocks and Fossils — Practice
blocks.intro: Answer every question, then check your answers. Open questions: compare your answer with the mark scheme and give yourself the marks you earned.

questions.q: A rock is made of rounded grains in layers. It has a shell fossil in it. What type of rock is it?
questions.e: Rounded grains, layers and fossils are all features of sedimentary rock.

questions.q: Which feature shows that a rock is igneous?
c: It has crystals lined up in stripes.
It has interlocking crystals in random directions.
questions.e: Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools; the crystals grow into each other in random directions. Stripes = metamorphic; fossils and soaking up water = sedimentary.

questions.q: Marble is a metamorphic rock. Which rock was changed to make marble?
questions.e: Heat and pressure change limestone into marble.

questions.q: (a) Which fossil is the oldest? Write the letter.
questions.e: C is in the lowest layer (layer 4). Layers are laid down one on top of another, so the lowest layer formed first and is the oldest.

questions.p:
Question 4
The diagram shows layers of rock in a cliff. Three fossils, A, B and C, are found in the layers. The layers have not been moved or turned over.
questions.q: (b) What type of rock are these layers made of?

questions.p:
Question 4
The diagram shows layers of rock in a cliff. Three fossils, A, B and C, are found in the layers. The layers have not been moved or turned over.
questions.q: (c) Explain why fossil C is older than fossil A.
questions.ms: 1 mark: layers of sediment are laid down one on top of another / new layers form on top. 1 mark: so the lower layer (layer 4) formed first / earlier than layer 1. Do not accept 'C is deeper' alone without the idea of layers forming in order (max 1).
questions.e: Sediment settles in layers, each new layer on top of the last. Layer 4 was laid down before layer 1, so the animal in it (C) lived and was buried before A.

questions.p:
Question 5
Sara tests three rocks, P, Q and R.
Rock P: grains rub off with a finger; water soaks in; layers can be seen.
Rock Q: very hard; random interlocking crystals; water stays on top.
Rock R: very hard; crystals lined up in bands; water stays on top.
questions.q: Which rock is metamorphic? Write the letter.
questions.e: Crystals lined up in bands is the feature of metamorphic rock. P is sedimentary; Q is igneous.

questions.q: Explain why fossils are almost never found in igneous rock.
questions.ms: 1 mark: igneous rock forms from melted rock / magma / lava. 1 mark: the (great) heat would destroy / burn / melt the remains (of the living thing). Accept 'too hot for remains to survive' for the second mark.
questions.e: Igneous rock forms when magma or lava cools. Melted rock is extremely hot, so any remains of plants or animals would be destroyed — there is nothing left to become a fossil.

questions.q:
These stages of fossil formation are in the wrong order.
A  Minerals slowly replace the bones.
B  An animal dies and sinks to the sea bed.
C  The rock is lifted up and eroded, so the fossil is exposed.
D  Mud quickly buries the bones.
Write the letters in the correct order.
questions.e: B (dies and sinks) → D (buried by mud) → A (minerals replace the bones) → C (uplift and erosion expose the fossil). Answer: B D A C.

questions.q: Why do most animals that die never become fossils?
c: They die on land, where there is no rock.
They rot or are eaten before they can be buried.
questions.e: To form a fossil the remains must be buried quickly. Most remains are eaten by other animals or rot away first.

questions.q: In a lake, about 1.5 mm of mud settles on the bottom each year. How many years would it take for a layer of mud 6 cm thick to build up?
questions.e: Change to the same unit: 6 cm = 60 mm. 60 ÷ 1.5 = 40 years.

questions.q: Limestone containing fossil sea shells is found in the desert near Cairo. What does this tell scientists about the area long ago? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the area was once (covered by) sea / under water. 1 mark: the shells came from sea animals that lived there and were buried in sediment (on the sea bed) which became rock. Accept: the land / rock was later lifted up or the sea moved away.
questions.e: Sea shells can only come from sea creatures, so the area was once under the sea. The shells were buried in sea-bed sediment that became limestone; later the sea disappeared and the land was left as desert.

questions.p:
Question 11
Ahmed weighs a rock sample. It has a mass of 120 g when dry. He soaks it in water for 30 minutes and weighs it again. Now its mass is 132 g.
questions.q: (a) Work out the mass of water the rock soaked up.

questions.p:
Question 11
Ahmed weighs a rock sample. It has a mass of 120 g when dry. He soaks it in water for 30 minutes and weighs it again. Now its mass is 132 g.
questions.q: (b) Which rock is Ahmed's sample most likely to be?
questions.e: The rock soaked up water, so it is porous. Sandstone is a porous sedimentary rock; granite, basalt (igneous) and slate (metamorphic) are not porous.

blocks.title: Remember
items: **Igneous** = melted rock cooled → random interlocking crystals, no layers, no fossils. Slow cooling = large crystals; fast cooling = small crystals.
**Sedimentary** = sediment in layers, pressed and cemented → grains, layers, often porous and soft, may contain fossils.
**Metamorphic** = existing rock changed by heat and pressure **without melting** → hard, crystals in bands, no fossils.
**Fossils** form when remains are buried quickly in sediment, layers build up into rock and minerals replace the hard parts; uplift and erosion expose them.
In undisturbed layers the **lowest layer is the oldest**.
